extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of medieval history; readers learning how to study and evaluate sources on the Crusades
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for historiographical study of the Crusades: how to select, classify, and weigh chronicles, narratives and other authorities, and how to frame claims about the Crusades' causes and results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer chronicles and narratives over documents for Crusade history
rubrics_metrics.description: In dealing with the literature of the Crusades, it is perhaps better, though ideally less scientific, to begin with chronicles and narratives rather than with documents. The history of a series of actions like the Crusades must primarily be based on these accounts; narratives must precede documents where one is dealing, not with the continuous life of an organized kingdom, but with a number of enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing events of the Crusades (which are episodic enterprises), give primacy to contemporary narratives and itineraria kept by crusaders. Use documents in support but not as the first basis for narrative reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study multiple cultural viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crusades must necessarily be studied not only in the Latin authorities of Europe and of Palestine, but also in Byzantine, Armenian and Arabic writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any serious account should consult sources from the varying perspectives (Latin/Western, Byzantine/Eastern Roman, Armenian, Arabic) to capture different angles and correct one-sided narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify First Crusade Western authorities into four kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking the Western authorities for the First Crusade separately, one may divide them, in the light of von Sybel's work, into four kinds--the accounts of eye-witnesses; later compilations based on these accounts; semi-legendary and legendary narratives; and lastly, in a class by itself, the 'History' of William of Tyre, who is rather a scientific historian than a chronicler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification as a framework for assessing provenance, reliability, and the type of material (eyewitness detail vs. later literary shaping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize contemporary eyewitness accounts where available
rubrics_metrics.description: The three chief eye-witnesses are the anonymous author of the Gesta Francorum, Raymund of Agiles, and Fulcher. The anonymous author of the Gesta was an eye-witness throughout and absolutely contemporary; Raymund and Fulcher are also contemporary and valuable for their respective points of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where contemporary eyewitness narratives exist, treat them as primary authorities for events (while still assessing bias and perspective). Examples given: Gesta Francorum (Norman layman/fighter perspective), Raymond of Aguilers (Provencal cleric/spiritual phenomena), Fulcher of Chartres (Lotharingian point of view).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate William of Tyre and other later authors cautiously for early events
rubrics_metrics.description: Until about 1840 the authority followed for the First Crusade was naturally the great work of William of Tyre. But Ranke suggested, and von Sybel proved, that Albert of Aix was not a good authority, and that consequently William of Tyre must be set aside for the history of the First Crusade, and other and more contemporary authorities used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not uncritically rely on later, learned historians (even 'scientific' ones) for reconstructing events where contemporary eye-witness accounts exist and where later writers may have incorporated legendary or derivative material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess value of a source by its contemporaneity, point of view, and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources differ in value because of their authors' social positions and perspectives (e.g., a lay Norman fighting in the ranks vs. a clerical Provencal), their proximity in time to events, and whether they were written as diaries/itineraria or later compilations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a source consider: contemporaneity (was the author present?), social/political standpoint (Norman, Provencal, Lotharingian, Italian mercantile), genre (diary vs. later redaction), and intended audience, all of which affect reliability and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and scrutinize later compilations and redactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The later compilations are chiefly based on the Gesta, whose uncouth style many writers set themselves to mend. There are plagiarists (e.g., Tudebod) and artistic redacteurs (Guibert of Nogent, Balderich of Dol, Robert of Reims) who confess indebtedness but reshape material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when a text is a reworking of an earlier account (smoothing style, adding material). Such works may be useful but should not be treated as independent eyewitness testimony; trace their dependence to primary texts where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about assigning broad social changes directly to the Crusades
rubrics_metrics.description: A cautious writer who seeks to find documentary evidence for every assertion may be rather inclined to attribute to that influence little or nothing. At most it may be admitted that the Crusades contributed to developments (dissolution of feudalism, development of towns, growth of scholasticism) rather than being their primary cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming long-term social, economic or intellectual effects for the Crusades, prefer documentary evidence and treat the Crusades as contributory factors among others rather than sole or deterministic causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on narrower, demonstrable results when seeking definite impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: If we seek the peculiar and definite results of the Crusades, we must turn to narrower issues: feudal colonization (younger sons, colonies like Jerusalem/Cyprus), chartered companies (military orders evolving into banks/navies), trade (emporia, trade routes), geography/discovery, military technology/adaptations, and systematic taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist of narrower topics as concrete loci for evidence-based claims about Crusade consequences (e.g., taxation precedents like Saladin tithe of 1188; trade routes from Venice to Bruges; military adaptations borrowed from the East).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat political uses of 'Crusade' rhetoric skeptically
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'Crusade' was sometimes used as a diplomatic or political convention to cover particular policies (e.g., the treaty of Granada 1500 excused as necessary in the interests of the Crusades). The papacy magnified its position through Crusades but was also corrupted by using Crusade rhetoric when there was no true holy war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering claims invoking Crusade motives or papal calls to arms, analyze whether the label masks dynastic, national or commercial interests and evaluate papal motives and outcomes critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: When cataloguing Crusade literature, distinguish collections vs. particular authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections (e.g., Bongars, Michaud, Recueil des historiens des croisades, publications of the Societe de l'Orient Latin) are valuable but vary in completeness and editorial quality; particular authorities (Gesta, Raymund, Fulcher, Annales Genuenses, Ekkehard, Raoul of Caen) have distinct strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard collections as starting points but check editorial quality and completeness; consult particular primary authors to understand their specific viewpoints and limits. Prefer editions noted in the text (Hagenmeyer, editions mentioned).
